---
title: "Life expectancy at birth in Portugal (platform test study)"
---

> **Note**: this is a **test** study for the platform, used to validate the `/estudo`
> pipeline end to end. It is not intended for publication as a substantive analysis, and
> the figures should be read together with the limitations described in the methodology
> section.

## Summary

Between [1960]{.claim id="c001"} and [2024]{.claim id="c002"}, life expectancy at birth in
Portugal rose from [64.0]{.claim id="c001"} to [82.5]{.claim id="c002"} years, in a nearly
continuous growth path over more than six decades. The gap between women and men stayed
relatively stable throughout the series: it was [5.6 years in 1960]{.claim id="c028"}
(women [66.7]{.claim id="c003"}, men [61.1]{.claim id="c004"}) and
[5.5 years in 2024]{.claim id="c029"} (women [85.2]{.claim id="c005"}, men
[79.7]{.claim id="c006"}). Portugal moved from being slightly below the average of the
European Union of twenty-seven at the start of the comparable series — [about 0.2 years
below in 2002]{.claim id="c032"} ([77.4]{.claim id="c007"} against [77.6]{.claim
id="c008"} years) — to being above it more recently — [about 1.0 year above in 2024]{.claim
id="c033"} ([82.5]{.claim id="c002"} against [81.5]{.claim id="c009"} years). The gap
between mainland NUTS II regions widened, from [0.8 years in 1992]{.claim id="c030"} to
[about 2.0 years in 2022]{.claim id="c031"}. Automatic break detection identified
seventeen candidate changes in the Portugal and EU series — [17]{.claim id="c020"} in
total —, of which [6]{.claim id="c020"} were linked to a concrete, dated event (almost all
related to the [COVID-19]{.claim id="c021"} pandemic) and [11]{.claim id="c020"} were recorded with no
identified event — a result of the verification process, not a failure of the analysis.

## Question 1 — Evolution of total life expectancy in Portugal

The longest available series (Eurostat, `demo_mlexpec`) shows an almost continuous increase
in life expectancy at birth in Portugal: from [64.0 years in 1960]{.claim id="c001"} to
[82.5 years in 2024]{.claim id="c002"}. The trend is interrupted by a few one-off
fluctuations (see Question 5), but the dominant pattern is one of sustained growth,
consistent with gradual improvements in sanitation, nutrition and access to healthcare
through the second half of the twentieth century and the start of the twenty-first.

```{ojs}
Plotly = require("plotly.js-dist-min@2.35.2")
```
```{ojs}
import {timeSeries, ranking} from "../../assets/charts.js"
```
```{ojs}
lang = "en"
```
```{ojs}
evolution_data = FileAttachment("life_expectancy_pt_eu.json").json()
```
```{ojs}
regional_data = FileAttachment("regional_evolution.json").json()
```
```{ojs}
snapshot_data = FileAttachment("regional_snapshot_2022.json").json()
```
```{ojs}
linked_events = FileAttachment("linked_events.json").json()
```

```{ojs}
viewof sex = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Total","T"],["Women","F"],["Men","M"]]), {value: "T", label: "Sex"})
```

```{ojs}
timeSeries(Plotly, evolution_data.filter((d) => d.sex === sex), {groupBy: "region", labels: {"União Europeia (27 países, 2020)": "UE-27"}, yTitle: "Years", events: linked_events, lang})
```

*Chart: life expectancy at birth in Portugal (total and by sex) and in the EU.*

## Question 2 — The gap between women and men

In nineteen sixty, life expectancy for women was [66.7]{.claim id="c003"} years, against
[61.1]{.claim id="c004"} years for men — a gap of [5.6 years]{.claim id="c028"}. More
recently, the values were [85.2]{.claim id="c005"} and [79.7]{.claim id="c006"} years,
respectively — a gap of [5.5 years]{.claim id="c029"}. Throughout the series this gap
stayed roughly constant, with no clear trend of convergence or divergence between the
sexes.

```{ojs}
timeSeries(Plotly, evolution_data.filter((d) => d.region === "Portugal" && d.sex !== "T"), {groupBy: "sex", labels: {F:"Women", M:"Men"}, yTitle: "Years", events: linked_events, lang})
```

*Chart: life expectancy at birth in Portugal, by sex.*

## Question 3 — Portugal against the European Union

In the first year for which the EU series is available in Eurostat, Portugal was slightly
below the European average: [77.4]{.claim id="c007"} years against [77.6]{.claim id="c008"}
years in [2002]{.claim id="c007"}, [a gap of about 0.2 years]{.claim id="c032"}. In the
most recent year of the series, the position reversed: Portugal was above the EU average,
with [82.5]{.claim id="c002"} years against [81.5]{.claim id="c009"} years in
[2024]{.claim id="c002"}, [a gap of about 1.0 year]{.claim id="c033"}. This suggests a path
of convergence followed by a slight advantage for Portugal over the European average in
the last two decades, although the aggregate EU indicator mixes countries with very
different trajectories.

## Question 4 — Regional differences (NUTS II)

Using the Eurostat annual series for the five mainland NUTS II regions, the gap between the
region with the lowest and the region with the highest life expectancy widened over time:
in [1992]{.claim id="c010"} it ran from [74.5]{.claim id="c010"} years in Norte to
[75.3]{.claim id="c011"} years in Alentejo — [a gap of 0.8 years]{.claim id="c030"}; by
[2022]{.claim id="c012"}, the relative position had reversed and the gap had widened,
running from [80.3]{.claim id="c013"} years in Alentejo to [82.3]{.claim id="c012"} years
in Norte — [a gap of about 2.0 years]{.claim id="c031"}. A more complete cross-sectional
picture from INE for the year [2022]{.claim id="c014"}, which also includes the autonomous
regions, shows an even wider gap: from [78.04]{.claim id="c014"} years in the Autonomous
Region of the Azores to [81.53]{.claim id="c015"} years in the Norte region.


```{ojs}
timeSeries(Plotly, regional_data, {groupBy: "region", yTitle: "Years", events: linked_events, lang})
```

*Chart: life expectancy at birth by mainland NUTS II region, annual series.*

```{ojs}
ranking(Plotly, snapshot_data, {xTitle: "Years", lang})
```

*Chart: life expectancy at birth by region, INE's cross-sectional picture for the most
recent year available in this source.*

## Question 5 — Breaks, slowdowns and the COVID-19 pandemic

Automatic break detection (see `quebras.csv`) identified [17]{.claim id="c020"} candidate
changes in the Portugal and EU series — level shifts, slope changes and spikes in the
year-over-year variation. Of those [17]{.claim id="c020"}, only [6]{.claim id="c020"} were
linked to a concrete, dated event with a credible source; the other [11]{.claim id="c020"}
were recorded with no identified event. This is treated as a result of the analysis, not a
failure: in several cases, namely isolated spikes in the older decades of the series and
level shifts in more recent years, no source establishes a concrete causal relationship
with a dated fact, even though plausible candidates were considered — political changes,
accession to economic blocs, economic crises and oil shocks. The detail of every candidate
assessed and discarded is documented in `ligacoes_eventos.csv`.

The clearest and best-documented break is the one at the start of the twenty-twenties. In
Portugal, total life expectancy fell from [82.0 years in 2019]{.claim id="c016"} to
[81.4 years in 2020]{.claim id="c017"} — [a break of about 0.6 years]{.claim id="c022"};
in the series used in this study for the EU, it fell from [81.1 years in 2019]{.claim
id="c018"} to [80.3 years in 2020]{.claim id="c019"} — [a break of about 0.8 years]{.claim
id="c023"}. The [COVID-19]{.claim id="c021"} pandemic, [declared by the World Health
Organization on 11 March 2020]{.claim id="c021"}, **contributed to** this break in
Portugal ([grade A]{.claim id="c022"}): this is the same year in which Eurostat, in its
*Statistics Explained* article on mortality and life expectancy, directly documents that
the pandemic **contributed to** a decline of [about 0.9 years (to 80.4 years)]{.claim
id="c023"} in life expectancy for the EU as a whole ([grade A]{.claim id="c023"}).
[This magnitude of 0.9 years]{.claim id="c023"}, published by Eurostat in a data version
that may already include later revisions, is not identical to [the 0.8 years]{.claim
id="c023"} computed directly from the `demo_mlexpec` series extracted for this study — the
difference reflects distinct data vintages between the Eurostat publication and the
extract used here, not two different phenomena. The subsequent recovery of life
expectancy in the EU over the following two years is also attributed by Eurostat to the
easing of the pandemic's acute impact (**contributed to** the recovery, [grade A]{.claim
id="c024"} and [grade A]{.claim id="c025"}).

A second, weaker-evidence candidate is the [severe 2014/2015 winter flu season in
Europe]{.claim id="c026"}, documented in an ECDC article on excess mortality among elderly
people in [14 European countries]{.claim id="c026"}. Since the article does not directly
quantify the effect on the EU's aggregate life expectancy indicator, this flu season **may
have contributed to** the negative spike observed in the EU series the following year
([grade B]{.claim id="c027"}), rather than a direct causal relationship being asserted.

It should also be noted that none of the candidates assessed but not confirmed (for
example, a European heatwave or a mild winter with no health crisis) was recorded as an
"event with no effect" because we found a source demonstrating the absence of an effect —
rather, we simply did not find a credible source establishing the effect, which is an
important distinction documented case by case in `ligacoes_eventos.csv`.

## Methodology and limitations

- The Portugal and EU series (total and by sex) come from Eurostat (`demo_mlexpec`),
  available annually since [1960]{.claim id="c001"} for Portugal and since [2002]{.claim
  id="c007"} for the European aggregate used. The regional NUTS II series come from a
  separate Eurostat dataset (`demo_r_mlifexp`), covered in this study between
  [1992]{.claim id="c010"} and [2022]{.claim id="c012"}.
- The more detailed regional picture, which includes the autonomous regions of the Azores
  and Madeira, comes from INE (indicator [`0008459`]{.claim id="c014"}). **This INE source
  was only confirmed as available for a single, recent cross-sectional period**, the year
  [2022]{.claim id="c014"}, at this stage of the study — it was not possible to confirm,
  within the scope of this test, a long historical series by region from this INE API,
  which limits our ability to compare the full regional evolution with the most recent
  year in the same source. For this reason, the two sources (Eurostat and INE) are
  presented in separate charts, rather than being merged into a single series.
- No INE source with a national-level breakdown by sex via a structured API was identified
  at this stage of data collection; that breakdown was covered only by the Eurostat source
  tested.
- Break detection uses three complementary methods (level shifts, slope changes and spikes
  in year-over-year variation), which explains why the most recent break shows up as a
  spike in the annual variation rather than as a long-term level shift.
- Links between breaks and events follow a confidence scale (grade A, B or C), and the
  language used in the text always reflects that grade: "contributed to" when a source
  directly establishes the causal relationship (grade A), "may have contributed to" when
  the mechanism is plausible but there is no direct demonstration of the effect on the
  indicator (grade B), and "coincided with" when there is only temporal coincidence with no
  source supporting a mechanism (grade C — not used in this study).
- As this is a platform test study, the number of questions and sources was kept small; it
  should not be read as an exhaustive analysis of the demographic literature on life
  expectancy in Portugal.
